content: 1. Assistance provided to a child must be tailored to their specific condition and the circumstances of their parents or caregivers. This assistance should be applied appropriately and effectively to meet the child’s needs. 2. Recognizing the unique needs of children with disabilities, any assistance provided under these conditions should be free of charge whenever possible. The financial resources of the parents or caregivers should be considered, and the assistance should aim to ensure the child has access to education, training, healthcare services, rehabilitation, preparation for employment, and recreational opportunities. These services should promote the child’s maximum social integration and individual development, including cultural and spiritual growth. 3. States Parties are encouraged to foster international cooperation by exchanging relevant information in the fields of preventive healthcare, medical, psychological, and functional treatment for children with disabilities. This includes sharing knowledge on integrating palliative care and symptom relief into pediatric care, as well as methods of rehabilitation, education, and vocational services. The goal is to enhance the capabilities and expertise of States Parties, particularly addressing the needs of developing countries. 4. States Parties acknowledge the child’s right to the highest attainable standard of health and access to facilities for treating illness and rehabilitating health. They must ensure that no child is deprived of access to necessary healthcare services. 5. To fully implement this right, States Parties must take measures to reduce infant and child mortality, provide essential medical assistance and primary healthcare, combat disease and malnutrition through available technology and adequate nutrition, ensure clean drinking water, and address environmental pollution risks. 6. States Parties must also ensure appropriate prenatal and postnatal healthcare for mothers, educate parents and children on child health and nutrition, promote breastfeeding, hygiene, and accident prevention, and develop preventive healthcare and family planning education. 7. Effective measures must be taken to abolish traditional practices harmful to children’s health. States Parties should also promote international cooperation to progressively realize the full implementation of these rights, with special attention to the needs of developing countries. 8. Every child has the right to a standard of living adequate for their physical, mental, spiritual, moral, and social development. Parents or caregivers bear the primary responsibility for securing these conditions within their abilities and financial capacities. 9. States Parties should assist parents and caregivers in fulfilling this responsibility by providing material assistance and support programs, particularly in areas such as nutrition, clothing, and housing. 10. States Parties must ensure the recovery of maintenance for the child from parents or others financially responsible, both domestically and internationally. This includes promoting international agreements and arrangements to secure such maintenance. 11. Early diagnosis and prompt, appropriate treatment, including pain relief and palliative care, can reduce mortality and improve outcomes and quality of life for children with cancer or other life-threatening conditions. 12. Child-friendly healthcare (CFH) standards aim to translate the principles of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child into practical healthcare practices. These standards provide a framework for assessing and improving healthcare to ensure children and their families receive the best possible care. 13. Pain and symptom management in children should involve dedicated services led by skilled health professionals and multidisciplinary teams. Written guidelines, evidence-based practices, and tools for symptom recognition and assessment are essential for effective care. 14. Essential drugs for symptom relief, including opioids, should be safely and affordably available. Non-pharmacological methods, such as distraction toys and psychological support, should also be utilized. 15. Individualized pain management plans should be developed in collaboration with children and their caregivers. Psychosocial support for children, families, and healthcare workers is crucial. 16. Routine procedures without pain relief, such as wound dressing, often cause unnecessary suffering. In some countries, children are sedated or paralyzed without adequate pain relief, which is ethically unacceptable. 17. States must ensure the availability of vital pain-relieving drugs, including opioids, and address outdated beliefs and misplaced concerns about their use in children. 18. Healthcare workers should prioritize pain relief, anticipate symptoms, and use both pharmacological and non-pharmacological methods to alleviate suffering. Training and education on pain management should be integral to healthcare practice. 19. Palliative care is essential for improving the quality of life for children with chronic or terminal illnesses. It focuses on symptom relief and making the present experience more bearable, rather than solely aiming for a cure. 20. Best practices in pediatric care involve planning individualized care, anticipating pain, using appropriate assessment tools, and administering drugs in a way that minimizes distress. Advocacy for the child’s needs and involving parents in care are also critical. 21. Non-drug measures, such as honesty, preparation, play, and comfort measures, can significantly alleviate a child’s suffering. Psychological support and kindness are equally important in managing distressing symptoms. 22. Palliative care improves the quality of life for patients and families facing life-threatening illnesses by addressing physical, psychosocial, and spiritual suffering. It is a fundamental, person-centered health service that respects the dignity and needs of patients.
